title: Manufacturing
subtitle: Bills of materials, work orders and the cost that ends up in finished goods
outcomes: Build a BOM that reflects how the product is actually made
Run work orders with material transfer, job cards and partial production
Explain the cost of a finished unit, and prove it
Subcontract without losing control of components

slides.title: Three documents, one idea
bullets: Bill of Materials: what a product is made of and the operations required, with costs and scrap
Work Order: a commitment to produce a quantity on a date, created manually or from a Sales Order or Production Plan
Job Card: the shop-floor work for one operation, recording time, operators and completion
A Stock Entry of type Manufacture consumes components and produces the finished good in one movement
slides.notes: Manufacturing in ERPNext is assembly with accounting attached. The BOM is the recipe, the work order is the batch, the job card is the labour record, and the manufacture stock entry is the physical event. If you remember that sequence, material, labour and cost questions answer themselves.

rows: What and how much per unit
How many, by when, in which warehouse
Time logs; cost via operation rate

slides.title: A BOM that survives the shop floor
bullets: Components carry quantity, rate, source warehouse and a scrap percentage — scrap belongs in the BOM, not in a monthly adjustment
Operations add time and cost per unit; without them, labour never reaches finished goods valuation
'Include Item in Manufacturing' distinguishes purchased components from sub-assemblies you build yourself
BOM cost is a snapshot: recalculate it deliberately when rates move, and keep old BOMs for audit
slides.notes: A BOM that omits scrap produces a work order that always comes up short, which the floor then fixes by issuing extra material with no document. Put the scrap percentage in the BOM even if it feels unflattering; it is the only way the variance report means anything. For multi-level products, explode the BOM and check that every sub-assembly has its own current version.

callout.title: Version the recipe
callout.text: New BOM version rather than editing a used one. Production history should point at the recipe that was actually used.

slides.title: From demand to a production plan
bullets: Sales Orders with a delivery date create the demand signal; Production Plan groups them per item and date range
Production Plan combines open work orders and stock on hand to suggest what to make and what to buy
Capacity planning compares work order hours against workstation availability — sales promises without it are fiction
Material Requests from the plan give purchasing a date-driven shopping list rather than a monthly guess
slides.notes: ERPNext does not pretend to be an advanced APS engine, and that is fine for most small and mid-sized plants. A weekly plan built from confirmed orders, current stock and open work orders beats a monthly spreadsheet, because it updates when reality changes. Keep the horizon short and the review cadence fixed.

slides.title: Running a work order without surprises
bullets: Transfer materials before consumption; Manufacturing Settings can backflush components based on the BOM or on transferred material
Partial production is normal: finished goods can be received in several entries against one work order
Rejected finished goods stay out of stock; record them as scrap or rework rather than receiving and adjusting later
Close the work order deliberately: material left unissued is either over-ordered or wasted, and both deserve a look
slides.notes: Work order discipline is mostly about timing. Materials issued too early inflate work in progress; production received before materials are issued creates negative component stock. Set the rule that no finished goods are received before the material transfer for that quantity, and make the shop floor's life easy enough that they follow it.

callout.title: Receiving without consuming
callout.text: Finished goods with no material issue understates cost of production and leaves components on the books. The stock ledger will show it.

slides.title: Job cards, time logs and capacity
bullets: Job Cards capture operator time against an operation; time logs aggregate for payroll and cost analysis
Workstation and operation rates turn minutes into money; without rates, labour stays a period expense
Hourly rate × time logged feeds additional costs on the work order if you enable it
Discipline beats precision: a rough time log recorded daily is better than a perfect one reconstructed monthly
slides.notes: If the shop floor will not log time, do not build a sophisticated costing model on top of fiction — cost labour at standard and treat the variance as overhead. The decision is cultural as much as technical, and it is worth having explicitly rather than discovering it in a margin review six months later.

slides.title: Where the unit cost comes from
bullets: Finished goods valuation = component value consumed + operation cost + additional costs, divided by accepted quantity
Component value uses the item's valuation method, so a wrong receipt price follows the product all the way to margin
Scrap and rejected quantity raise the cost of the good units — which is correct, and worth showing to production
Work in progress is the gap between materials issued and finished goods received; review it for work orders left open
slides.notes: Costing arguments end when you can walk the arithmetic: these components at these rates, this many minutes at this rate, this much extra, divided by this many good units. Build that walk-through once for a real product and keep it as a worked example. If the number does not match, you now know which of the four inputs to check.

rows: Wrong receipt rate or missing landed cost
Landed cost or journal against the work order

slides.title: Subcontracting without losing the components
bullets: Mark the BOM as subcontracting, raise a Purchase Order for the service, and transfer components to the subcontractor warehouse
Receipt of the finished good consumes the transferred components — the subcontractor never owns them on your books
Value the service charge into the finished good via the purchase invoice or a landed cost on the receipt
Reconcile the subcontractor warehouse monthly: components sent minus consumed must equal stock held outside
slides.notes: The subcontractor warehouse is a real place with real risk. Treat it as an audit area: a monthly statement of components held, signed by the supplier, is the only thing that keeps the numbers honest. If you skip that, the first stocktake will produce a variance you cannot explain.

slides.title: Five manufacturing reports worth reading
bullets: Work Order Summary — open, overdue and completed by item and date
Production Analytics — quantities produced against planned, by period
BOM Cost / Stock Balance — confirm the recipe cost matches today's component prices
Work In Progress — issued material not yet received as finished goods, by work order
Capacity / Workstation analysis — hours promised against hours available
slides.notes: Read the work-in-progress report before any inventory review; it is where forgotten work orders hide. Overdue work orders are a customer promise problem, not a manufacturing one, so share that report with sales. Production analytics only becomes useful once scrap and rejection are recorded, which is why chapter discipline matters.

callout.title: Sales tax on manufactured goods
callout.text: Sales tax applies at the point of sale, not production. Keep manufacturing value movements out of SST accounts; tax belongs on the invoice.

lab.title: Manufacture a product and prove its cost
steps: Create two component items and one finished item; add a BOM with 2 units of each component, 5% scrap and one operation of 30 minutes
Set a workstation hourly rate and confirm the BOM cost shows material plus operation cost
Create a Work Order for 10 units from a Sales Order; transfer the required materials to WIP
Create a Job Card for the operation, log 4 hours, and complete it
Receive 9 finished units (one rejected) against the work order; note the valuation rate and explain why it exceeds the BOM cost
Run Work In Progress and Work Order Summary; close the work order and confirm no material remains unissued
Compare the finished item's valuation to the BOM cost and write a one-line reconciliation of the difference
lab.done: You can state the cost of one good unit and account for every component, minute and rejected unit behind it.

quiz.question: Which document consumes components and creates finished goods?
quiz.why: The manufacture stock entry is the physical and accounting event; the work order only authorises it.

quiz.question: Why does a BOM need a scrap percentage?
options: So material planning and cost reflect real consumption rather than ideal consumption
quiz.why: Without scrap in the BOM, work orders are always short and the floor issues undocumented extra material.

quiz.question: Finished goods were received before any material transfer. What is the symptom?
options: Negative component stock and understated cost of production
quiz.why: Receiving production without consuming components leaves components on the books and pushes stock negative.

quiz.question: In subcontracting, where do components sit while the supplier works on them?
options: Transferred to a subcontractor warehouse that you still own and reconcile
quiz.why: Ownership does not transfer; the subcontractor warehouse is your stock location and needs a monthly reconciliation.

quiz.question: Which report localises forgotten work orders holding material?
quiz.why: Work In Progress lists material issued but not yet received as finished goods, per work order.

narration: Chapter seven is manufacturing, which in ERPNext is assembly with accounting attached. Three documents and one idea. The bill of materials is the recipe: components, quantities, operations, scrap and cost. The work order is the batch: how many, by when, from which warehouse. The job card is the labour record. Then a stock entry of type manufacture is the physical event that consumes components and produces finished goods. Put scrap in the BOM even when it feels unflattering. Without it, every work order comes up short and the shop floor quietly issues extra material with no document, which destroys the variance report. Version your BOMs instead of editing recipes production already used, so history points at the recipe that was followed. Plan from confirmed orders through a production plan, and check capacity before promising dates. When executing, transfer materials before consuming, receive finished goods in partial entries as reality requires, and record rejected units rather than receiving and adjusting later. Receiving production before consuming components is the classic error: it leaves component stock negative and understates cost of production. Cost per finished unit is components consumed, plus operations, plus additional costs, divided by accepted quantity; when it looks wrong, check those four inputs in that order. Reconcile subcontractor warehouses monthly, and read work in progress before every inventory review.
